_about: Spoiler-free dramatis personae plus a names/forms-of-address note and a pinyin pronunciation guide, rendered as a front-matter page by build_reading_epub.py (render_cast). Each figure is described by the role in which the reader first meets them: surface identities only, no hidden allegiances, deaths, romances-as-reveals, or plot turns. 'pron' is a rough English respelling (approximate; the guide teaches the real sounds). Keep blurbs short. The novel's characters are the author's invention (see the translator's note).
lead: A guide to the principal figures, each described by the role in which the reader first meets them, with a rough guide to saying the names below. All are the author's invention; their world is real.

address.title: Names and forms of address
paras: Chinese names put the family name first: Chen Qianli is Mr. Chen, and his brother is Chen Qianyuan (the two share the family name Chen and differ only in the given name, so watch the last syllable).

The same person is often addressed, not by name, but by a warm tag: Old before a surname for a familiar senior or an equal (Old Fang is Fang Yunping, Old Yi is Lu Zhongde), Little or Young for a junior, and Master for a skilled tradesman (Master Dong the chef). Officials go by rank (Section Chief Mu, Secretary Ma, Director Ye, Captain You).

Both sides also use work names and code names as a matter of routine. A code name such as Haohan stands in for a person whose real identity is kept dark, and an operative may be known to different people by different names. When a name shifts, it is usually the same person under a new mask, not a new character.

pronunciation.title: Saying the names
pronunciation.intro: Pinyin, the romanization used here, spells a few sounds in ways that surprise English readers. The respellings above and here are rough guides, not exact; these are the letters that trip people up.
sounds: ‘dz’ and ‘ts’: z as in ‘kids,’ c as in ‘cats.’
i (after zh, ch, sh, r, z, c)
a buzzed vowel close to ‘r’: Lin Shi is ‘lin shr,’ Sinan is ‘sz-nahn.’
ü, and u after j, q, x, y
‘ee’ said with rounded lips: yun is ‘yün.’
